title: Feature Bagging Provides Stability
claim: Subsampling can occur along instances, features, or both, and ensembles apply these schemes repeatedly across components of a larger learner.
layout: 4 panels left-to-right; matrix cartoons (a-c) then tree diagram (d)
description: Four panels. Panels (a) to (c) each show a response column Y and a feature matrix X as white rectangles. In (a), instance subsampling is shown by green horizontal-striped feature columns. In (b), feature subsampling is shown by yellow vertical-striped row bands in both Y and X. In (c), the two combine, and the overlap region is blue crosshatch. Panel (d) is a larger orange-bordered diagram of bagging in a random forest. It shows Tree 1 through Tree B, separated by an ellipsis. Each tree has an instance-subsampling box at the top, with an arrow down to a tree of Root, Split and Node ovals. Red Split nodes link to gray callout bubbles that show per-split feature subsampling. Captions sit under each panel. The eye goes first to the colored striped matrices on the left.
caption: Illustration of subsampling and bagging schemes. In the random forest example (d), all splits within a single tree share the same instance subsample (yellow lines), while each split uses an independently drawn feature subsample (green columns).
abstract: We study feature bagging through the lens of algorithmic stability. Feature bagging is an ensemble strategy that aggregates base learners trained on randomly subsampled feature subsets, possibly in a data-dependent manner. We introduce feature instability (FI), the feature-axis analogue of instance instability (II), which measures sensitivity to removing a single feature. Smaller values of II or FI correspond to stronger stability, and our experiments show that FI captures generalization-relevant information complementary to II. Within this framework, we analyze feature bagging in both a parametric linear model and a model-free setting inspired by recursive feature subsampling in random forests. In both settings, we establish formal guarantees showing that feature bagging improves the relevant stability relative to its non-bagged counterpart, with larger improvements under more aggressive subsampling. We further show that a modest number of bagging rounds is sufficient to approach the infinite-bagging stability level.
